newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Cock fighting a passion for Filipinos.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cock fighting a passion for Filipinos.

text.p: It is Sunday morning and Elpidio Acebal rushes towards the Santa Quiteria Cockpit in Novaliches, a poor district in suburban Manila.
Employed as a driver at a Manila company, Acebal is one of thousands of ordinary Filipinos whose money goes to making cock fighting, the second biggest gambling business in the country.
The number one business is an illegal numbers game called jueteng (pronounced hwe-teng).
Cock fighting is legitimate business in the Philippines and is so popular that women often complain that husbands care more about the fowl than their wives.
This Sunday morning, Acebal is willing to bet up to 500 pesos ($19), a lot of money in a poor country where the average daily wage for a labourer is 130 pesos ($5).
"Kut Kut Boy looks good. You want to put money on him," says Acebal, his eyes sharpening as he closely considers the strutting fowl's bristled feathers and aggressive posture.
In the less than 10 minutes allotted before the fight, bets on Kut Kut Boy in the small arena have gone up to 10,000 pesos ($382).
The scale gives some indication of how state-owned Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp (PAGCOR) has become be the country's most profitable company.

In 1995 PAGCOR, whose income comes from taxing cock fighting and other popular passions like horse racing and lotteries, earned a record profit of 5.9 billion pesos ($225 million). Its profits surged by 25 percent over 1994 when it was seventh in the list of top profit-making companies.
There is a deafening roar as Kut Kut Boy wins and those who bet on him exult in victory.
Cock fighting is serious business for bettors as well as cock owners who spend months preparing for a fight.
What distinguishes a winner from the ordinary bird is its "hot blood," says Acebal who owns four such fighting cocks.
Training mainly consists of getting two fowls excited and then letting them charge headlong at each other.

Their diet is supplemented with vitamin capsules and "Thunderbird Electrogen" which, according to a blurb for the product, "contains electrolytes that rapidly replace lost body fluids and maintains liveliness".
Keeping the bird in darkness for about 24 hours before the fight ensures it is in the meanest of moods before the fight.
"It's nice when your cock wins, sometimes the prize can be as high as 5,000 pesos ($190)," says Gorio Agbay, who is unemployed and supported by his wife working as a maid in Cyprus.

Afficionados like Agbay dream of the day they will win a derby, perhaps the biggest which is held at the Araneta Colosseum, where 30,000 fans saw Muhammad Ali stop Joe Frazier in a 1975 bout that is still remembered as the "Thrilla in Manila".
At the Santa Quiteria Cockpit, where the annual derby was held in August, the champion cock's owner took prize money of 90,000 pesos ($3,435). The champion himself barely survived.

In cock fighting, the winner sometimes dies but the owner takes the prize because his cock has had the last peck in a fight which lasts less than a minute and to the untrained eye seems like just a blur of blood and feathers.

The cocks are armed with two-inch long curved stainless steel daggers tied to their feet. A headlong crash into each other followed by random swipes of the dagger ensures that one or sometimes both cocks soon collapse.
The referee holds them by the neck and if both cocks peck, the fight is not over yet. Another brief bout of stabbing each other and the fowl that can still peck its rival wins.

Amid the deafening din of winning bettors and downcast losers, the birds are taken backstage where a "doctor" sits, fully equipped with knives, scissors, needle and thread, swabs of cotton and an antiseptic liquid.

A quick gash with the knife opens the wounds sufficiently for doctor to lift the skin and clean the insides with cotton held at the tip of two fingers. A stitch completes the job and the cock is taken home to convalesce.

About 10 feet (three metres) away a rusty tin of boiling water sits on an open fire. The dead and dying go in here and, for a small price, a boy will strip the skin and clean it, ready to be taken home and cooked.
